title: Building This Room
excerpt: How I rebuilt my portfolio as a room you can walk into, on top of an open-source foundation, and the small details that took the longest.
body:
## Why a room

My old portfolio was a page of sections. It listed the right things, but it didn't feel like anyone lived there. I wanted a site where you walk into my space first and read about my work second.

Henry Heffernan's portfolio does this beautifully: a 3D room, a camera that glides onto the desk, and a working computer on the screen. So I didn't start from zero. I forked his open-source room and desktop and rebuilt them around me.

## What I kept, what I changed

I kept the part that makes it work: the camera journey from the room to the desk to the screen, and a desktop with real draggable windows.

Almost everything else changed:

- The old CRT became a space-black MacBook Pro that starts closed and opens as the camera approaches.
- The empty studio became my room: a Barça flag behind the desk, Messi's Barcelona and Argentina shirts beside the TV, a turntable, bean bags and a bed.
- The desktop became a macOS-style workspace, with a dock, a menu bar and a Finder-like portfolio.
- Begu, the AI chatbot from my old site, became a husky who walks around the room. Click him and you can ask about my work.

## Details that took the longest

The hard parts were never the big features. They were small things that looked wrong:

- The laptop lid sat about ten millimetres behind the base when closed, and only opened halfway from far away. The fix was calibrating the hinge and opening the lid by camera state instead of distance.
- A live mirror re-rendered the whole room every frame and made the site lag. Swapping it for a cheaper reflective surface, and capping the pixel ratio, brought it back to a steady 60 FPS.
- Click sounds got loud after rapid typing, because dozens of effects stacked up and never disconnected. Capping overlapping sounds at four and cleaning them up fixed it.

## Things to find

The room rewards a second look. The turntable opens Music, the bookshelf opens these notes, and a few record sleeves are hidden around the room. Each one you find plays its album.

## What I learned

Building on someone else's foundation is a skill of its own. Most of the work was reading code I didn't write, deciding what to keep, and making every change feel like it belonged. That is not far from what building with AI systems is like: the interesting part is rarely starting from scratch.

title: Building AI Agents That Actually Work
excerpt: A practical guide to building multi-agent systems that go beyond demos. Learn the patterns and pitfalls from real production deployments.
body:
## Introduction

After spending the past year building and deploying AI agent systems in production, I've learned that the gap between a working demo and a reliable system is enormous. This post shares the hard-won lessons from building agents that actually work.

## The Agent Illusion

Most AI agent demos follow a predictable pattern:

1. Show a complex-sounding task
2. Agent "thinks" and makes tool calls
3. Magic happens, task complete

What they don't show is the **failure modes**. Real agents fail in spectacular ways:

- Infinite loops when the model gets confused
- Hallucinated tool calls that crash your system
- Context windows overflowing with irrelevant information
- Costs spiraling as the agent explores dead ends

## Building Robust Agents

Here's what actually works:

### 1. Constrain the Action Space

Don't give your agent unlimited tools. Start with the minimum viable toolset:

```python
tools = [
    search_knowledge_base,  # Read-only, safe
    create_draft,           # Creates but doesn't publish
    request_human_review,   # Escalation path
]
```

Notice the pattern: **read operations are safe, write operations require review**.

### 2. Implement Circuit Breakers

Every agent needs guardrails:

```python
class AgentGuardrails:
    max_iterations: int = 10
    max_tool_calls: int = 20
    timeout_seconds: int = 120
    cost_limit_usd: float = 0.50
```

When any limit is hit, the agent stops and escalates. No exceptions.

### 3. Make Failures Visible

The worst agent bugs are silent failures. Instrument everything:

- Log every LLM call with full context
- Track token usage per request
- Monitor success rates by task type
- Alert on unusual patterns

## The Multi-Agent Trap

Multi-agent systems sound elegant: specialized agents collaborating! In practice:

> "Every agent you add is another point of failure."

Start with a single, well-designed agent. Only split when you have clear evidence that:

1. Tasks are genuinely independent
2. Specialized prompts significantly improve performance
3. You can handle coordination overhead

## What I'd Do Differently

If I were starting over:

1. **Start simpler** - One agent, three tools, clear scope
2. **Invest in evaluation** - Build your test suite before your agent
3. **Design for failure** - Every agent action should be reversible
4. **Monitor aggressively** - You can't fix what you can't see

## Conclusion

Building AI agents that work in production isn't about the fanciest architecture or the newest model. It's about **ruthless simplicity**, **aggressive monitoring**, and **designing for failure**.

The best agent is often the one that knows when to ask for help.
